claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Sharp interphase boundaries in the starting alloy cause pronounced dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
A controlled low-temperature aging treatment will induce nanoscale coherent precipitates selectively along internal lamellar boundaries.
Boundary nanoprecipitates will modify the interfacial structure.
Boundary nanoprecipitates will reduce the mechanical mismatch between the two phases.
The nanoprecipitates will act as intermediate sites that promote more uniform dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
More uniform dislocation transmission will prevent severe dislocation pile-ups and reduce local stress concentrations.
Reduced interfacial stress concentration will delay microcrack initiation.
The altered interfacial behavior will inhibit rapid crack propagation.
The aging treatment will increase room-temperature elongation to failure relative to the untreated alloy.
The aging treatment will maintain or slightly improve yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The aging treatment will maintain or slightly improve ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy has limited tensile ductility and undergoes brittle fracture because of dislocation pile-ups at sharp internal boundaries.
The beneficial response depends on optimizing precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Over-aging or non-uniform precipitation may reduce strength or cause softening.
The proposed effect is intended to apply under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading.
The treatment is to be rejected if elongation does not improve by more than 10% relative to untreated controls.
The treatment is to be rejected if microscopy does not confirm targeted nanoprecipitate formation at the lamellar boundaries.
The treatment is to be rejected if it produces an undesirable reduction in strength.
